course_information.title: Merchandising Fundamentals
course_information.description: Learn how clear product presentation, accurate shelf information, and thoughtful displays help customers shop confidently.
course_information.intended_audience: All employees; especially sales floor, merchandising, and department associates
course_information.scope: General; store-specific policies must be supplied separately
course_information.restrictions: No authority to perform inventory adjustments, investigations, detentions, security review, equipment operation, or price overrides without store authorization.
learning_objectives: Explain how merchandising helps customers find and compare products.
Match products to accurate shelf labels and approved locations.
Describe simple display principles including visibility, organization, and safety.
Identify common merchandising problems and appropriate corrections.
Use customer questions and observations to improve displays through approved processes.

lessons.title: See the Store Through the Customer’s Eyes
lessons.objective: Understand how product presentation affects shopping.
lessons.why_this_matters: Merchandising is the way a store organizes and presents products for customers. Good merchandising helps a shopper find the right item, compare choices, and understand what else a project may require.

content_sections.heading: Make products easy to find
content_sections.text: Clear categories, readable signs, and organized shelves reduce confusion. Customers should not need to guess where related items are kept.

content_sections.heading: Help customers compare
content_sections.text: Group products according to the store’s approved plan. Make differences such as size, use, and package count visible.

content_sections.heading: Keep information accurate
content_sections.text: A tidy display is not helpful if the shelf label belongs to another product.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A shopper needs a paint roller. The associate points to a section where roller covers are arranged by size and type, with clear labels.
what_to_say_or_do: Walk an aisle as a first-time shopper would.
Check whether categories and labels make sense.
Report confusing signs or mixed products.
common_mistakes: Using an attractive sign that is hard to read.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a department lead before changing the store’s layout or category grouping.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Walk an aisle as a first-time shopper would.
Check whether categories and labels make sense.
Ask a department lead before changing the store’s layout or category grouping.

practice.question: What is the main purpose of good merchandising?

options.text: Make every shelf look full at any cost.
Help customers find and understand products.
Hide slower-selling items.
Reduce employee conversations.

lessons.title: Match Products, Locations, and Shelf Labels
lessons.objective: Keep merchandise and price information aligned.
lessons.why_this_matters: Shelf tags and signs should identify the product actually displayed. Similar packages can vary in size, quantity, finish, or price. Always check the item identifier rather than guessing from appearance.

content_sections.heading: Read the details
content_sections.text: Confirm SKU or barcode, description, size, unit, and price display according to store policy. If the label seems wrong, request verification before replacing it.

content_sections.heading: Follow the approved plan
content_sections.text: A planogram is a diagram or guide showing where products should be placed. Not every store uses one. Follow the store’s approved shelf arrangement or manager direction.

content_sections.heading: Avoid misleading displays
content_sections.text: Do not place a product under a price or promotion sign that applies to something else. Refer uncertain price questions to authorized staff.

lessons.hardware_store_example: Two tubes of adhesive have similar packaging but different uses. The associate checks each item against its shelf tag before filling the hooks.
what_to_say_or_do: Match the product identifier to the shelf label.
common_mistakes: Placing products based on package color.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask the pricing or merchandising lead when the tag, price, or placement does not match.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Match the product identifier to the shelf label.
Ask the pricing or merchandising lead when the tag, price, or placement does not match.

practice.question: Two products look alike but have different SKUs. What should you do?

options.text: Place them together behind one tag.
Match each SKU to its approved shelf label.
Choose the label with the lower price.
Remove both labels.

lessons.title: Build Useful and Safe Displays
lessons.objective: Recognize practical display principles and safety limits.
lessons.why_this_matters: A display should make a product easy to see and select without creating a hazard. Good displays balance visibility, clear information, accessibility, and safe storage.

content_sections.heading: Show the purpose
content_sections.text: A small project display can group related items, such as a paint tray, roller cover, painter’s tape, and drop cloth. Keep labels and prices clear for each product.

content_sections.heading: Respect safe limits
content_sections.text: Do not stack heavy or unstable products beyond approved limits. Keep exits, safety equipment, and walking routes clear. Ask for authorized help with ladders or powered equipment.

content_sections.heading: Keep it shoppable
content_sections.text: Customers should be able to take a product without pulling down a pile or disturbing another display. Replace damaged packaging through approved procedures.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A fall cleanup display pairs leaf bags with gloves and rakes. The team checks that the products are secure and the display does not narrow the aisle.
what_to_say_or_do: Use approved display fixtures and locations.
Show related products with clear individual labels.
common_mistakes: Blocking a walkway with promotional merchandise.
Creating a display without accurate price information.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a manager about fixture limits, heavy merchandise, or new display locations.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Use approved display fixtures and locations.
Ask a manager about fixture limits, heavy merchandise, or new display locations.

practice.question: Which display is most helpful?

options.text: An unstable tower of products.
A clear project display with accurate labels and open walkways.
Mixed products with one price tag.
A display blocking a fire extinguisher.

practice.explanation: Useful displays are clear, accurate, and safe.

lessons.title: Maintain Shelves and Seasonal Areas
lessons.why_this_matters: Displays need attention after customers shop them. Empty hooks, mixed products, damaged packages, and outdated signs can confuse shoppers.

content_sections.heading: Recover the aisle
content_sections.text: Recovery means returning products to their proper locations and straightening shelves. Check item labels as you go rather than pushing everything forward without looking.

content_sections.heading: Check promotions
content_sections.text: Use the current approved promotion information. Remove or report outdated signs according to store procedure. Do not promise a promotion that cannot be verified.

content_sections.heading: Think seasonally
content_sections.text: Seasonal products should be easy to find when demand rises. Follow the approved calendar and layout. Do not move stock into a new location without approval.

lessons.hardware_store_example: After a weekend sale, an associate finds spring seed packets mixed into fall lawn-care supplies. They sort them into approved locations and flag an expired sign.
what_to_say_or_do: Report empty locations and expired signs.
Follow the approved seasonal merchandising plan.
common_mistakes: Leaving an expired sale sign up.
Moving seasonal stock without telling the team.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a manager about promotional timing, seasonal resets, or unavailable replacement signs.

supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Report empty locations and expired signs.
Ask a manager about promotional timing, seasonal resets, or unavailable replacement signs.

practice.question: You notice an expired promotion sign. What is the best response?

options.text: Leave it because it looks nice.
Verify and follow the approved sign-correction process.
Promise the discount anyway.
Move it to another aisle.

practice.explanation: Current, accurate signs reduce customer confusion.

lessons.title: Improve Displays Using Customer Questions
lessons.objective: Use simple observations to identify display improvements.
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers show us where merchandising is confusing. Repeated questions about a location, size, or difference between products can point to a sign or layout problem.

content_sections.heading: Notice repeated questions
content_sections.text: If several shoppers cannot find the same product, check whether the location or sign is clear. One question does not prove the layout is wrong.

content_sections.heading: Share a specific suggestion
content_sections.text: Describe the customer problem and a possible improvement. Example: “Three shoppers asked where hose washers are. Could we add a clearer sign near the hose fittings?”

content_sections.heading: Make changes with approval
content_sections.text: Managers may consider space, inventory, brand requirements, and safety before approving a new sign or display. Do not change prices or permanent layouts on your own.

lessons.hardware_store_example: Customers regularly ask which sandpaper grit to choose. An associate suggests an approved comparison sign that explains grit ranges in plain language, subject to product accuracy review.
what_to_say_or_do: Request approval before changing fixtures or permanent signs.
common_mistakes: Changing prices to make a display simpler.
Adding unverified technical claims to signage.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a manager to review new signs, product claims, or layout changes.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Ask a manager to review new signs, product claims, or layout changes.

practice.question: Several customers cannot find hose washers. What is a useful next step?

options.text: Ignore the questions.
Move the washers without telling anyone.
Suggest a clearer sign or location to the department lead.
Tell customers to search harder.

practice.explanation: Specific feedback can guide an approved improvement.
